clue.text: What's the point of class distinction on board ?

definitions.text: What's the point of class distinction on board ?

parts.words: What's the point of class distinction on board
parts.note: at old dining tables guests of rank sat above the condiment holder and lesser folk 'below the salt', so the item on the table board marked the dividing point

explanation.surface: A question about what purpose social snobbery serves aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a ship, but the board is the dining table; sitting 'below the salt' meant a lower social rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The vessel holding salt on a table historically divided the high-ranking diners from the rest.

clue.text: Decoration for Bob at the top of the tree

indicators.note: in a down entry, the shilling letter sits above the tree word, so it comes first

parts.note: a bob is old British slang for a shilling, abbreviated s
the ash is a common tree

explanation.surface: Someone called Bob hangs an ornament at the very top of the Christmas tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a name but is a shilling, the old British coin written s; the shilling letter goes at the top of the tree, ASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of ribbon worn over the shoulder is an honour or ornament, such as an order of chivalry.

clue.text: Face up to being put down

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading upwards turns the word for face backwards

parts.note: a dial is the face of a clock or watch

explanation.surface: Confronting the indignity of being humbled or insulted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face up to' reads as 'confront', but 'up' alone signals that DIAL is written upwards in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laid has been placed or set down on a surface.

clue.text: Sheraton for P.M. ?

explanation.surface: Comparing an eighteenth-century furniture designer with the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Sheraton was a famous English furniture designer; a Prime Minister 'makes' a cabinet by choosing ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheraton crafted fine furniture for a living, and a premier appoints the senior government ministers who form a Cabinet.

clue.text: Time to go down to a place not far from London

definitions.text: Time to go down to a place not far from London

parts.words: Time to go down to a place not far from London
parts.note: echoes Alfred Noyes's poem 'The Barrel-Organ': go down to Kew in a certain springtime blossom season, 'it isn't far from London'

explanation.surface: Advice on when to visit somewhere near London.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes a refrain of the poem 'The Barrel-Organ', which names a flowering shrub's season; Kew, home of the botanic gardens, is the place near London.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's refrain calls spring at Kew the season of this purple-flowered shrub's blossoming.

clue.text: Genuine cut in heat processing

indicators.note: processing works the letters of the words before it into a new form

explanation.surface: A real reduction in heating, achieved by some industrial process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Processing' rearranges all the letters of CUT IN HEAT, including the 'in', which is fodder rather than a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something real and not counterfeit.

clue.text: One of the continental dates

parts.note: points to a fixed day in the calendar of ancient Rome, a continental European city, such as the fifteenth of March

explanation.surface: A remark about a date in a European calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman calendar counted from three fixed days a month, and this one fell in mid-month; 'continental' points to Rome on the European continent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman calendar named the middle day of each month this way, as in the famous March date.

clue.text: Record our time of life, in order to get us down ?

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record
your age is your time of life

explanation.surface: Writing down our age just to make us gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'get us down' (to depress) is a loose verb phrase for dishearten.
explanation.definitionFit: Disheartening someone is getting them down, lowering their spirits.

clue.text: Hangers in the dressing-room

parts.note: hangers suggest coat-hangers in a wardrobe, but means things that hang down from clothing as one dresses

explanation.surface: Coat-hangers kept in a changing room.
explanation.walkthrough: Hangers suggests coat-hangers; the actual hangers are the flaps that dangle from a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: The lower loose flaps of a shirt hang down below the waist when untucked.

clue.text: Jephthah's stream said to be fatal to Ephraimites

definitions.text: Jephthah's stream said to be fatal to Ephraimites

parts.words: Jephthah's stream said to be fatal to Ephraimites
parts.note: in Judges 12, Jephthah's men tested fugitives with a Hebrew word for a stream, killing those who mispronounced it

explanation.surface: A biblical reference to a deadly river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hebrew word means stream or ear of corn; Ephraimites could not say its 'sh', so saying it was a test. 'Said' is the pun: the word is lethal when spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Now any password or custom that marks out members of a group, from the biblical test word.

clue.text: Drunk from a stirrup-cup ?

definitions.note: a past participle standing for a wine, something that is drunk

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Tipsy after the farewell drink offered to a rider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like tipsy but means something that is drunk; the wine is taken from 'a stirrup', a stirrup-cup being a drink for a departing rider.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparkling Italian wine from Piedmont is something drunk.

clue.text: A race with trouble and strife? A sound if misleading clue

definitions.text: A race with trouble and strife? A sound if misleading clue

parts.words: A race with trouble and strife? A sound if misleading clue
parts.note: the Derby horse race sounds like the man's name, and 'trouble and strife' is Cockney slang for wife, giving a man and his wife

explanation.surface: A clue admitting it pairs a horse race with marital discord.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is an English horse race pronounced 'Darby'; Cockney rhyming slang 'trouble and strife' means wife. The clue confesses it sounds right but misleads, since the couple are devoted, not quarrelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a devoted elderly married couple, from an old ballad.

clue.text: Suffered the rough and tumble of travel

definitions.text: Suffered the rough and tumble of travel

parts.words: Suffered the rough and tumble of travel
parts.note: reads as being jostled on a journey, but also means having roamed about the world

explanation.surface: Someone was bruised and shaken on a rough journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means both roughly treated and having wandered widely, and the clue combines the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Being battered and being a wanderer who has roamed casually from place to place share one idiom.

clue.text: Wilfully cut out ?

parts.note: wilfully suggests deliberately, but means by way of a testament, removing an heir

explanation.surface: Something deliberately removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilfully' reads as deliberately but means by a will: being cut out of a will.
explanation.definitionFit: Excluding someone from receiving an inheritance in a testament.

clue.text: Arachne's parlour

parts.note: Arachne was turned into a spider in Greek myth, and the rhyme says 'Will you walk into my parlour?' said the spider to the fly

explanation.surface: The sitting room of a mythological weaver.
explanation.walkthrough: Arachne was a Greek weaver turned into a spider; the nursery poem has the spider invite the fly into her 'parlour', her trap.
explanation.definitionFit: The arachnid's silken trap is the parlour of Mary Howitt's poem.

clue.text: A pint — Time ! So can't wait

annotationWithheld.why: A pint—Time! So can't wait (9): the answer is an anagram of A PINT TIME, but no clue word signals the rearrangement ('So' is a link), so the anagram has no indicator to annotate
annotationWithheld.clue: A pint — Time ! So can't wait

clue.text: Throw out, in a manner of speaking

definitions.text: Throw out, in a manner of speaking

parts.words: Throw out, in a manner of speaking
parts.note: the verb comes from Latin for hurling a javelin and also means to exclaim, so it is throwing out words

explanation.surface: Expelling something, figuratively speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' looks like a hedge, but literally means by speech: the verb's old sense is to blurt out words.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb, from Latin for throwing, means to utter suddenly, casting out words.

clue.text: Morning massage, then a turn in the country

indicators.note: giving the run of letters a turn reverses the order of the whole piece

parts.note: to rub is to massage

explanation.surface: A morning massage followed by a stroll in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Then a turn' reads as a walk, but it turns the whole AMRUB backwards; 'the country' is the definition, not countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Asian nation now called Myanmar.

clue.text: It's less than 2,000 miles in diameter

definitions.text: It's less than 2,000 miles in diameter

indicators.note: the answer is a smaller run of letters lying within the longer phrase that follows

explanation.surface: A country's width given in miles.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a country about that wide, and the answer is spelt inside 'miles in diameter'.
explanation.definitionFit: The subcontinent nation measures roughly that distance across.

clue.text: Port for Michael

explanation.surface: A drink of port intended for someone called Michael.
explanation.walkthrough: Port reads as the drink; it is the Russian White Sea harbour, and Michael is the chief angel in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Arkhangelsk is a northern Russian harbour city, and Michael is a chief angel in scripture.

clue.text: Pantalunacy ?

parts.note: a made-up blend of pantomime, Pantaloon and lunacy, suggesting the madcap comic part of an old pantomime

explanation.surface: An invented word for theatrical madness.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantaloon was a stock character in the comic section of Victorian pantomimes, alongside Harlequin and Columbine.
explanation.definitionFit: The slapstick part of a traditional pantomime, featuring the clown figure in diamond-patterned costume.

clue.text: No nodding poet, he !

parts.note: taken as written
a nod signals agreement, a yes

explanation.surface: Insisting that a particular poet never dozes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No nodding' reads as staying awake, but 'nodding' is the assent YES; Alfred Noyes was an English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Noyes wrote 'The Highwayman' and other popular verse.

clue.text: A man of account

explanation.surface: Describing a man of note or importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A man of account' sounds like a person of standing; read as man's name plus account.
explanation.definitionFit: William is shortened to a familiar name, and a statement of charges owed is an invoice.

clue.text: "I… owe no man hate, no man's happiness " said Corin

definitions.text: "I… owe no man hate, no man's happiness " said Corin

parts.words: "I… owe no man hate, no man's happiness " said Corin
parts.note: the shepherd Corin's line in As You Like It has a word missing before 'no man's happiness'

explanation.surface: A quotation from a shepherd in Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: Corin, in As You Like It, says he owes 'no man hate, — no man's happiness': fill in the missing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Resenting another's good fortune is the feeling Corin disclaims.

clue.text: Commotions in the ranks

explanation.surface: Disturbances among soldiers in the lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Pronounced to rhyme with cows it means quarrels; to rhyme with toes it means lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisy quarrels and lines of things in order are spelt alike.

clue.text: The new arrival has a pound on Caledonian, or Nebuchadnezzar for instance

parts.note: a newborn child is a new arrival
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra
taken as written
Ian is a typically Scottish name, and Caledonia is Scotland

explanation.surface: A newborn is given money on a Scottish occasion, alongside a biblical king.
explanation.walkthrough: Caledonian looks like an adjective but stands for a Scot, IAN; Nebuchadnezzar was king of Babylon.
explanation.definitionFit: The king was ruler of the ancient Mesopotamian empire based in Babylon.

clue.text: Have a bath with a musical instrument

parts.note: to tub is an old verb for bathing

explanation.surface: Bathing while playing a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: TUB as a verb means to bathe.
explanation.definitionFit: A large brass instrument with a deep pitch.

clue.text: You can't take it with you-not really

definitions.text: You can't take it with you-not really

parts.words: You can't take it with you-not really
parts.note: property you cannot take to the grave, and in law movable goods as opposed to real estate, called realty

explanation.surface: The proverb about wealth staying behind at death, with a doubtful afterthought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not really' looks like a casual aside but means 'not realty': lawyers divide property into land (realty) and movable goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal term for personal property, movable possessions rather than land.
